newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar romps ahead despite calls for calm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar romps ahead despite calls for calm.

text.p: The dollar stormed ahead against the mark on Monday, oblivious to official calls for calm as traders fretted about the weak German economy and the single European currency.

With U.S. markets closed for the President's Day holiday, European shares drifted aimlessly, with London and Germany closing lower as investors took profits from a long bull run, and Paris ending marginally higher.
But the action was on the foreign exchange market where the dollar romped to 1.70 marks for the first time since April 1994.
With New York closed, European buying was not strong enough to carry the dollar through 1.70 but by the close it was just a fraction below at 1.6997 marks.
"The outlook for the dollar is still positive, in view of continued economic problems in Germany and Japan," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
A worry for the market is the economic state of Germany and whether this will have a knock-on effect on European economic and monetary union (EMU) which is scheduled for 1999.

With German unemployment at the highest level since the 1930s, doubts are growing whether Bonn can cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, a key criterion for EMU membership.
EMU is inconceivable without Germany, by far the European Union's biggest economy and one of the most enthusiastic supporters of the euro single currency.
The German State Secretary for Finance Juergen Stark insisted on Monday that the deficit target would be met. But not everyone on the financial markets believes him.

"There's a risk premium related to the uncertainty on what's going to happen to the mark and what kind of euro we'll have and when, and until this issue is clarified it will almost always be negative for the deutschemark," said Giorgio Radaelli, senior international economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
Bundesbank Vice President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum became the latest European official to try to slow the dollar's relentless climb, saying he saw no reason for a weaker mark.

Speaking to Reuters on a visit to India, Gaddum said he understood why investors were attracted by the dollar at present, but did not believe the currency markets were seeing the full picture of future expectations.
"There is no reason for a weaker deutschemark," he said. "I am not looking for strength for the dollar, I am looking for the strength, possible future strength of the deutschemark."
But his comments had little effect.
The dollar also firmed against the yen. It was quoted at 124.50 yen at the European close, up from 124.22 on Friday.
But dealers said the dollar's gains against the yen were limited by concerns that central banks -- notably the Bank of Japan (BOJ) -- might intervene to stem its rise.
Intervention fears were stoked overnight by a news agency report that Japan and the United States had agreed that the BOJ could intervene if the yen dropped sharply.

Share markets, by contrast, had an uneventful day. British, German and French stocks all fell in the morning following a weaker Friday close on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones Industrial average ended down 33.48 points at 6,988.96.
But the early profit taking fizzled out and they clawed back most of their losses, with Paris closing slighly higher.

In London the FTSE 100 index, which hit a record close on Friday, ended down just 3.1 points at 4,337.9 as investors shrugged off a parliamentary vote scheduled for Monday night which is aimed at toppling the Conservative government.

The opposition Labour Party will try to bring down the government with a vote expected around 2200 GMT on whether to censure Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg over his handling of the mad cow disease crisis.
If Prime Minister John Major lost, there could be a confidence vote in the government the next day. If he lost that vote, Major would have call an early general election.
Major is expected to survive the Monday night vote and he has to call an election by May in any case. But politics may soon play a bigger role as Labour is far ahead in opinion polls.

"One day it will dawn on the market that there's going to be a change in government, and the market probably will get quite choppy as a result," said UK equity strategist Robert Buckland of HSBC James Capel.
German stocks likewise fell on profit-taking after 11 consecutive record closes. The DAX index closed down 15.61 points at 3,232.57 and German dealers welcomed the drop.
"Everyone here is hoping that the market will fall back so that taking new positions will be cheaper. After 11 record days, a breathing space will do nothing but good," said one dealer.

Profit-takers pushed down the Paris market in the morning but the CAC 40 index recovered to close up 7.06 at 2,634.48. Car maker Renault fared less well, falling 2.94 percent after warning last week that its losses would be worse than the market expected.
CURRENCIES AT 1700 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6997 marks and 124.50 yen compared with 1.6878 marks and 124.67 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 3.1 points at 4,337.9.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed up 7.06 at 2,634.48 points.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed 15.61 points lower at 3,232.57.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $344.25 an ounce after being fixed at $344.10 in the afternoon and compared with Friday's close of $343.05. Silver was at $5.21, up five cents from Friday's close.
